question: A 53-year-old man comes to the emergency department for severe left knee pain for the past 8 hours. He describes it as an unbearable, burning pain that woke him up from his sleep. He has been unable to walk since. He has not had any trauma to the knee. Ten months ago, he had an episode of acute pain and swelling of the right great toe that subsided after treatment with indomethacin. He has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, psoriasis, and hyperlipidemia. Current medications include topical betamethasone, metformin, glipizide, losartan, and simvastatin. Two weeks ago, hydrochlorothiazide was added to his medication regimen to improve blood pressure control. He drinks 1–2 beers daily. He is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall and weighs 110 kg (242 lb); BMI is 38.1 kg/m2. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F). Examination shows multiple scaly plaques over his palms and soles. The left knee is erythematous, swollen, and tender; range of motion is limited by pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Gout flare -> Severe left knee pain -> Unbearable, burning pain -> Woke him up from sleep -> Unable to walk -> No trauma to the knee -> 80% CHAIN: Gout flare -> Acute pain and swelling of right great toe 10 months ago -> Treated with indomethacin -> 70% CHAIN: Gout flare -> Hyperuricemia -> Increased serum uric acid levels -> 90% CHAIN: Gout flare -> Psoriasis -> Scaly plaques over palms and soles -> 80% CHAIN: Gout flare -> Erythematous, swollen, tender left knee -> Limited range of motion -> 80% CHAIN: Gout flare -> Possible tophi formation -> 70% CHAIN: Gout flare -> Management with arthrocentesis -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most appropriate next step in management for the 53-year-old man with severe left knee pain and a history of gout flare is arthrocentesis. The patient's presentation is consistent with a gout flare, supported by the acute pain and swelling of the right great toe 10 months ago, which was treated with indomethacin. Arthrocentesis is indicated for diagnosis and management of gout flares, especially in the presence of erythematous, swollen, and tender joints with limited range of motion.
analysis: The patient's presentation is highly suggestive of a gout flare, given his history of acute pain and swelling in the right great toe, which responded to indomethacin. Arthrocentesis is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis of gout and guide management.
